quote: Any politician who’d said “6,000 deaths is 1/8 the annual US casualties from automobile accidents,” would have been asked to resign the same hour.
content: One out of 519. The Authorization for Use of Military Force passed the Senate 98–0 and the House 420–1, and Barbara Lee was the one. She needed a security detail for the death threats. She survived politically in one of the safest seats in the country, Oakland and Berkeley, and 534 other members of Congress made the calculation the essay describes and voted yes. A single exception from the most insulated district in the United States confirms the spiral: restraint was speakable at a price that only an electorate uniquely sheltered from the pressure would pay. "No one would dare" was hyperbole by one vote. The rally effect Fable cites is the essay's mechanism, measured (Mueller 1970).

quote: If the USA had completely ignored the 9/11 attack—just shrugged and rebuilt the building—it would have been better than the real course of history.
content: The essay understated its own case by three orders of magnitude, as Fable says: trillions of dollars, not billions. Brown University's Costs of War project puts direct deaths in the post-9/11 war zones at over nine hundred thousand. On the counterfactual, the adversary had already stated the plan. In his October 2004 video, bin Laden described al-Qaeda's aim as "bleeding America to the point of bankruptcy," provoking the United States into costly wars by sending "two mujahidin" to "raise a piece of cloth" wherever it wished the generals to race. For a null response to have been worse, al-Qaeda would have needed hundreds of further 9/11s. The essay's "walk straight into al-Qaeda's trap" is its enemy's strategy in the enemy's own words.
